name: Nebraska
note: In Nebraska the funeral director and embalmer in charge of the funeral fills out the death certificate, the attending physician, physician assistant or nurse practitioner signs the medical part electronically within 24 hours, and the certificate goes to the Department of Health and Human Services (the State Registrar) within five business days. In Omaha and Lincoln it goes first to the city-county health department. The county attorney is the ex officio coroner: deaths with no attending practitioner or suspected violence go to them, and they sign every cremation permit. State law sends the death on in only a few places: DHHS gives each election official a death list every three months, the federal statistics service gets the data, and Medicaid estate recovery hears through the probate notice to creditors. Copies are limited to people with a 'proper purpose' as defined by DHHS rule.

steps.title: Refer unattended or suspicious deaths to the county attorney
steps.who: The funeral director and embalmer, when no physician, physician assistant or nurse practitioner attended the death; any death possibly caused by neglect, violence or unlawful means. The county attorney is the ex officio county coroner.
steps.trigger: Death with no licensed practitioner in attendance, or circumstances suggesting neglect, violence or unlawful means.

deadline.text: county attorney states the cause within twenty-four hours after taking charge

steps.summary: The county attorney, who acts as coroner, investigates and signs the death certificate electronically. If the cause is not yet known, the certificate is filed to record the fact of death, and supplemental cause information follows within six weeks. Sudden unexpected deaths of children aged one week to three years need an autopsy before any cause is certified.

steps.title: Complete and electronically sign the medical certificate of death
steps.who: The physician, physician assistant or nurse practitioner who last attended the deceased.
steps.trigger: The death of an attended patient.

deadline.text: within twenty-four hours from the time of death

steps.summary: The attending practitioner completes the 'medical certificate of death' part of the certificate and signs it by the electronic means the department provides.

steps.title: File the death certificate with DHHS (State Registrar)
steps.who: The funeral director and embalmer in charge of the funeral, who fills out the personal particulars, including the decedent's social security number.
steps.trigger: The death; completion of the medical certification.

deadline.text: within five business days after the date of death

steps.summary: A completed certificate must reach the Department of Health and Human Services within five business days. If that is impossible, the funeral director tells the department why and files as soon as possible. Refusing to perform a duty under the Vital Statistics Act is a Class I misdemeanor.

steps.title: In Omaha and Lincoln counties, file with the city-county health department
steps.who: Persons in a county containing a city of the metropolitan or primary class with its own birth and death registration system (Douglas and Lancaster).
steps.trigger: A death in such a county.

deadline.text: within five business days of the date of the death

steps.summary: These counties are exempt from filing directly with the department: certificates go to the local vital statistics office.

steps.title: Local health department forwards certificates to DHHS
steps.who: The city-county or county health department vital statistics office.

deadline.text: within ten business days of the date of the death

steps.summary: The local office forwards the certificates to the state department.

steps.title: County attorney signs the cremation permit
steps.who: The county attorney (or a designated representative) of the county where the death occurred.
steps.summary: No body may be cremated until the county attorney has signed a cremation permit electronically, on a form the department prescribes. Transit permits out of the state are issued by the funeral director, but need the county attorney's authorisation when the death is under investigation.

steps.title: Certified copies to applicants with a proper purpose
steps.who: Applicants with a 'proper purpose' as defined by rule: the registrant's spouse, child or parent; the legal representative (including the personal representative) for legal purposes such as probate, property transfer, insurance or benefits; funeral homes for the family within one year; law enforcement; government; media; and genealogists after 50 years.
steps.trigger: An application with proof of identity and of a proper purpose.
steps.summary: DHHS issues a certified copy or an 'abstract of death' (no signatures) for a $16 fee. The applicant carries the burden of proving a proper purpose. The fee may be waived for Social Security benefit claimants facing hardship, and is waived for veterans' claims.

steps.title: Match deaths to birth records and exchange with other states
steps.who: DHHS, with vital records offices outside Nebraska.
steps.summary: To prevent fraudulent use of a dead person's birth certificate, DHHS may post the fact of death to the birth record and exchange death records with other states. Birth certificate copies of deceased persons are marked 'deceased'.

steps.title: Mortality statistics and release to the federal statistics service
steps.who: DHHS, to its own statistics function, the United States Public Health Service (national vital statistics) and approved researchers.
steps.latencyNote: no time set (nrs-71-616; nrs-71-602; 174 NAC read)
steps.summary: DHHS tabulates statistics from all registered deaths. It may release the confidential statistical part of the certificate only to the US Public Health Service, government health agencies or approved researchers.

steps.title: Quarterly death list to election commissioners and county clerks
steps.who: DHHS sends the list to each election commissioner or county clerk, who may remove a deceased voter on any supporting information.
steps.trigger: Deaths of residents in the county over the quarter.
steps.summary: DHHS must provide, at cost, a record of deaths of residents in each county every three months. Election officials may also remove a registration at any time on other supporting information about the death.

steps.title: Death data to government agencies for fraud prevention
steps.who: Federal, state, county or municipal agencies, for preventing fraud or waste of government funding; state agencies doing automated review of certificates.
steps.summary: DHHS may disclose certificate data to government agencies for limited anti-fraud purposes, at cost. Other state agencies pay cost for automated review of death certificates and abstracts rather than per-copy fees. The death certificate also carries the decedent's social security number for child support enforcement.

steps.title: Probate notice to DHHS for Medicaid estate recovery
steps.who: The party instituting the probate proceeding, when the decedent was 55 or older or lived in a medical institution.
steps.trigger: Appointment of a personal representative and publication of notice to creditors.
steps.latencyNote: runs from appointment: "within five days after the first publication" (nrs-25-520-01)
steps.summary: The notice to creditors must also go to DHHS (which runs Medicaid) with the decedent's social security number, delivered in the way DHHS posts on its website (which may be email). A notice that does not conform is void.

steps.title: Final Nebraska income tax return
steps.who: The executor, administrator or other person charged with the care of the decedent's property.

deadline.text: when it would have been due had the decedent not died

steps.summary: The Department of Revenue learns of the death through the final return filed by the estate. No statute found sends vital records data to it.

steps.title: No state route for banks or insurers; narrow search for medical societies
steps.who: The Nebraska Medical Association, its allied medical societies or in-hospital staff committees (peer-review studies). No equivalent route exists for financial institutions.
steps.summary: DHHS must search death certificates for medical peer-review bodies and give non-certified copies for up to $3 per search. Otherwise private bodies rely on a certified copy that the family or legal representative obtains as a 'legal use'.

steps.title: Published notice to creditors
steps.who: The clerk of the county court, on appointment of a personal representative.

deadline.text: first publication within thirty days after the appointment

steps.summary: A notice runs once a week for three weeks in a county newspaper, and creditors must present claims within two months of first publication.

registrationDeadlineDays.note: Five business days after death (§ 71-605(3)); the same in Douglas/Lancaster counties via the local health department (§ 71-608.01).

informantDuty.note: The funeral director and embalmer in charge of the funeral causes the certificate to be filled out and filed. No next-of-kin informant duty in statute.

medicalExaminerScrutiny.note: No independent review of every certificate. The county attorney (ex officio coroner) takes unattended or suspicious deaths and must sign every cremation permit.

electronicRegistration.note: Statute requires the medical certificate and cremation permits to be signed electronically. The text read here does not require the whole certificate to be filed electronically.

centralPopulationRegister.note: No population register; the death record is kept by DHHS as State Registrar, which preserves all certificates permanently.

governmentPropagation.note: Under state law, registration reaches election officials automatically through a quarterly DHHS death list, and the statistics function. Medicaid estate recovery learns through the probate notice, not from vital records. No state statute was found that sends deaths to the DMV or the Department of Revenue. Federal benefit payers are reached through the us-federal layer (SSA).

certificateAccess.note: Certified copies only for a 'proper purpose' defined by rule (close family, legal representative, funeral home, government, media, genealogists after 50 years). Public records may be viewed at the DHHS office.

gaps: No Nebraska statute was found on who may pronounce death. Chapter 71 vital statistics sections 71-601 to 71-649 and the chapter 71 index were read; the Uniform Determination of Death Act location was not checked.

dhhs.ne.gov (and www.dhhs.ne.gov) refused the session (CONNECT 403), so DHHS's death-certificate and electronic death registration (EDRS) guidance could not be read. Whether funeral directors must file the whole certificate electronically is not established.
Pointer § 32-318 is about voter signatures, not deaths. The death-removal provision is § 32-327, which is cited instead.

No state statute or rule was found requiring vital records to notify the DMV (driver licence cancellation) or the Department of Revenue of deaths. The chapter 60 and 77 catchline indexes were searched for death terms.
No Nebraska statute or rule read here mentions an electronic death feed to SSA. It is left to the us-federal layer.
174 NAC ch. 3 was read through the rules.nebraska.gov JSON API (the site is a single-page app with no stable chapter URL), so the citation URL is the API endpoint for Title 174.

privateSectorVerification is left to the us-federal layer (LADMF). State law gives no route for banks or insurers; the only private search route is for medical peer-review bodies under § 71-612(5), shown as step ne-private-none.
